primitives.name: Second-Order Drive Mechanism
primitives.verbatim_quote: The Second-Order Drives The second-order drives may be roughly characterized as demands to get to or from certain relatively general environmental situations, plus certain more or less specific sign-gestalt-readinesses as to how to get thus to and from.
primitives.assumptions: Drive activation depends on perceived utility to first-order appetites; sign-gestalt readiness is contextually encoded.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When environmental utility becomes negligible or inverted relative to first-order appetites.

layer2.mapping: D_2(E_g, S_g) encodes strategic behavioral intent derived from proximal cues and long-term motivational alignment.
layer2.telemetry: Observable behavioral consistency with environmental goal-seeking patterns.

primitives.name: Drive Utility Alignment
primitives.verbatim_quote: Further, they are to be characterized by the fact that such demanded, or to-be-avoided, general environmental situations are ones which are likely to prove useful in the long run as means to any or all of the firstorder appetites and aversions.

primitives.assumptions: Long-term utility is a probabilistic measure of alignment between D_2 and F_1.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When U(D_2, F_1) approaches zero or negative values.

layer2.mapping: U(D_2, F_1) models the causal kernel linking drive activation to motivational reinforcement.
layer2.telemetry: Behavioral persistence under repeated environmental exposure to aligned stimuli.

primitives.name: Docile vs Autonomous Drive Hypothesis
primitives.verbatim_quote: Two Possibilities: (a) the Second-Order Drives Are Docile; (b) They Go Off in Their Own Right Granting that the second-order drives do thus usually tend to prove ancillary to the first-order drives, there are, nevertheless, two alternative hypotheses as to the true nature of this relationship.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'H_docile': 'Hypothesis of docility (binary)', 'H_auto': 'Hypothesis of autonomy (binary)', 'R(D_2, F_1)': 'Reactive relation between D_2 and F_1 (dimensionless)'}
primitives.assumptions: H_docile = 1 iff R(D_2, F_1) is positively correlated; H_auto = 1 otherwise.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When reactive relation R(D_2, F_1) becomes stochastic or non-monotonic.

layer2.mapping: H_docile(H_auto) determines whether D_2 is conditionally activated by F_1 or independently evolves.
layer2.telemetry: Temporal correlation between drive onset and first-order appetite change.

reasoning_traces.think:
Second-order drives are defined as higher-order motivational mechanisms that orient behavior toward general environmental states based on anticipated long-term utility to first-order appetites. These drives are not directly tied to immediate satisfaction but rather to strategic positioning within an evolving motivational landscape. The mechanism operates through sign-gestalt readiness—cognitive templates encoding how to navigate toward or away from environmental situations. This process is modeled as a conditional utility maximization where D_2(E_g, S_g) is activated when E_g aligns with F_1’s long-term utility. The dual nature of these drives manifests in two hypotheses: either they are docile, responding only when utility is confirmed, or autonomous, operating independently of such confirmation. In the docile case, activation ceases when utility diminishes, while in the autonomous case, activation persists regardless of outcome. This duality introduces a bifurcation in behavioral predictability, requiring dynamic Bayesian inference to model activation likelihood. The failure mode occurs when environmental utility becomes misaligned or undefined, leading to maladaptive or erratic behavior. The system's robustness depends on maintaining stable mappings between D_2 and F_1, ensuring that sign-gestalt readiness remains predictive of future motivational success.
